snippet.title: Dan Snow On The Second Great Fire of London
snippet.description:
On December 29th, 1940, London faced a night of destruction that rivaled the Great Fire of 1666. As the Luftwaffe rained tens of thousands of incendiary bombs upon the "beating heart of the Empire," St Paul’s Cathedral stood at the center of a firestorm. This documentary takes you on a tour through the modern streets of London to uncover the scars of the Blitz. From the "Heroes with Grimy Faces", the volunteer firefighters and taxi drivers who fought the flames, to the iconic photograph that gave a war-torn nation hope, we explore how strategic decisions, sheer bravery, and a touch of luck saved London’s most famous landmark from total annihilation.

snippet.title: Fall Asleep to the ENTIRE Story of the Great Fire of London 1666 — The City in Flames
snippet.description:
This video tells the story of The Great Fire of London, the disaster that reshaped England’s capital in the 17th century.

In September 1666, a small fire began in a bakery on Pudding Lane and spread rapidly through the narrow streets of London. Strong winds, wooden buildings, and crowded neighborhoods allowed the flames to move unchecked, forcing thousands of residents to flee with only what they could carry. Churches, homes, and landmarks were reduced to ash as the fire burned for several days.

Although the destruction was vast, the loss of life was surprisingly low. In the aftermath, London faced the slow task of rebuilding, leading to wider streets, new building regulations, and a transformed city. Figures such as Samuel Pepys left behind detailed personal accounts that help us understand how ordinary people experienced the fire.

This gentle bedtime history explores the Great Fire of London as a moment of destruction followed by renewal, showing how a city endured loss and quietly began again.

Great Fire of London: The Untold Story You all know the story about the Great Fire of London. That the fire was started by accident in a bakery on Pudding Lane, and the inferno rapidly engulfed the City of London in September 1666, burnt for four days, destroying everything in its path. snippet.title: A Tour of London Before the Great Fire of 1666
snippet.description:
A Tour of London Before the Great Fire of 1666 takes you into a city that believed it had survived the worst history could offer. Narrow streets lean inward. Timber houses breathe smoke and warmth. Markets, taverns, churches, and river trade pulse with confidence and routine.

This cinematic historical documentary explores London as it existed on the eve of destruction—a dense, wooden city shaped by habit rather than design. Fire is everywhere, trusted and familiar. Authority is divided. Regulations exist on paper but not in practice. Life continues comfortably, unaware that comfort itself has become the danger.

Through immersive visual storytelling and historically grounded narration, this film traces how London lived, worked, traded, and slept before a single spark revealed the fragility beneath its strength. The Great Fire is not treated as sudden fate, but as an event decades in the making.

This is not a story about flames alone.
It is about cities, systems, and the illusion of safety.

Because what London learned in 1666, modern cities still risk forgetting today.

The Great Fire of London 🔥 | How One Spark Destroyed a City (1666 Documentary)


In 1666, one of the most devastating fires in human history reduced London to ashes.
What began as a small spark in a Pudding Lane bakery quickly became a blazing inferno that consumed over 13,000 homes, 87 churches, and St. Paul’s Cathedral — changing the city forever.

In this cinematic documentary, we uncover:
🔥 The real cause behind the Great Fire of London
🏙️ How the city’s wooden architecture and narrow streets fueled the flames

snippet.title: What Was London Like During the Great Fire of London (1666)
snippet.description:
Step into London in September 1666—one year after the Great Plague—when a city of timber, pitch, and crowded medieval streets became a single, unstoppable flame. What began as a spark in a baker’s shop on Pudding Lane turned into four days of chaos, wind-driven firestorms, and collapsing order as London’s narrow lanes became wind tunnels and its riverside warehouses became fuel.

This episode is a cinematic reconstruction of the Great Fire of London through eyewitness accounts like Samuel Pepys and John Evelyn. Using historical detail and AI visualization, we recreate the frantic evacuations along the Thames, the extortion and looting that followed the breakdown of authority, and the moment the medieval St. Paul’s Cathedral—thought to be safe—was consumed in molten lead and exploding stone.

Witness the turning point when royal power finally intervened, buildings were blown apart with gunpowder to create firebreaks, and the city’s survival demanded sacrificing entire neighborhoods. From the refugee fields outside the walls to the rebirth of London in brick and regulated streets, this is the story of how a catastrophe didn’t just destroy a city—it redesigned it, creating the foundations of modern building codes, fire insurance, and professional firefighting.

London didn’t simply survive the fire. It became something new in the ashes.

snippet.title: The Great Fire of London
snippet.description:
The Great Fire of London was a major conflagration that swept through central London from Sunday 2 September to Thursday 6 September 1666, gutting the medieval City of London inside the old Roman city wall, while also extending past the wall to the west. The death toll is generally thought to have been relatively small, although some historians have challenged this belief.
The fire started in a bakery in Pudding Lane shortly after midnight on Sunday 2 September, and spread rapidly.

snippet.title: A Day In London, 1666 (THE GREAT FIRE: 3 Days That Changed A City Forever)
snippet.description:
Spend a day in London, September 1–3, 1666 — starting in Pudding Lane, where the fire begins, then racing along the warehouses of Thames Street, through Cheapside’s busy market, and toward Old St. Paul’s as the Great Fire of London tears through a tightly packed wooden city. You’ll see why the flames spread so fast: a hot, dry summer, narrow streets, overhanging timber houses, and riverside stores of tar, tallow, coal, and spirits that turned whole blocks into fuel.

Built from eyewitness diaries (Samuel Pepys and John Evelyn), parish and Fire Court records, and period maps and engravings, and reconstructed with modern AI video tools, this immersive walk rebuilds the Great Fire hour by hour — the first spark in Farriner’s bakery, the explosions on the waterfront, the collapse of churches and guildhalls, and the refugee camp at Moorfields as rumors spread and the skyline burns.

snippet.title: The History of London Fire Brigade (1666-1985) | From the Great Fire to the Blitz & Beyond
snippet.description:
Welcome to London Fire Brigade Archives, our new series where we dig into the vault and showcase historical footage of the London Fire Brigade. This exclusive collection brings never-before-released vintage videos, offering a glimpse into the evolution of firefighting in London.

For our first release, we’re featuring "The Men and Women of London Fire Brigade," a documentary produced in 1985. This 18-minute film takes you on a journey from the Great Fire of London in 1666 through key moments in LFB history, leading up to the state of firefighting in the 1980s.

 What You’ll See in This Video:
📌 The Formation of the London Fire Brigade:
Early days of fire protection (insurance brigades, private firemen)
Establishment of the London Fire Engine Establishment in 1833
The Great Fire of Southwark (1861) and its impact
The official formation of the London Fire Brigade in 1865

📌 Evolution Through the Decades:
London Fire Brigade in 1965, including the shift to modern control systems
The role of the National Fire Service (NFS) during WWII, including stories of heroism during the Blitz
The last horse-drawn fire engines being retired in 1921

📌 Firefighting in 1985 – Equipment & Specialist Units:
A look at the brigade’s hose layer, fire boat, damage control units, TLS, and support units

How London’s firefighting force operated in the 80s, including the five branches at HQ:
• Operations
• Technical Services
• Brigade Support
• Personnel & Administration
• Fire Prevention

📌 The Core Mission of LFB:
Saving lives
Protecting property from fire
Providing humanitarian services

This documentary is a fascinating time capsule of the London Fire Brigade’s rich history. Stay tuned for more archive footage as we explore the past of the UK’s busiest fire service!

The destruction of St. Paul’s Cathedral and entire parishes

The panic, rumors, and resilience of ordinary people

How London rose again from the ashes, forever changed

The Great Fire was more than a tragedy—it was a turning point. This is the story of survival, loss, and rebirth.

snippet.title: The Great Fire of London: A Timeline of Tragedy | Medieval Documentary
snippet.description:
Today we thought we would travel outside of the Middle Ages and into the early modern period. But why? We hear you shout when you have 1,000 years of medieval history to go at. Well, the answer is easy. The Great Fire of London was one of the greatest catastrophes ever to befall the City and was a tale just too extraordinary not to be told. Over ffour days from Sunday 2nd to Wednesday 5th September 1666, London was over powered by the largest and fastest moving fire that it had ever faced. 

Fanned by easterly winds, it spread quickly across the city, like a relentless predator, consuming everything in its path. When the wind eventually dropped and the flames finally guttered out, the devastation was clear to see, causing the famed diarist Samuel Pepys to state that it was “the saddest sight of desolation that I ever saw”. Welcome to Early Modern Madness.
